title: Celsus offers other heroes
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα τοίνυν, πρὸς ἃ κατὰ δύναμιν ἀπηντήσαμεν, φησὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς· πόσῳ δ᾿ ἦν ὑμῖν ἄμεινον, ἐπειδή γε καινοτομῆσαί τι ἐπεθυμήσατε, περὶ ἄλλον τινὰ τῶν γενναίως ἀποθανόντων καὶ θεῖον μῦθον δέξασθαι δυναμένων σπουδάσαι; φέρε, εἰ μὴ ἤρεσκεν Ἡρακλῆς καὶ Ἀσκληπιὸς καὶ οἱ πάλαι δεδοξασμένοι, Ὀρφέα εἴχετε, ἄνδρα ὁμολογουμένως ὁσίῳ χρησάμενον πνεύματι καὶ αὐτὸν βιαίως ἀποθανόντα. ἀλλ᾿ ἴσως ὑπ᾿ ἄλλων προείληπτο. Ἀνάξαρχον γοῦν. ὃς εἰς ὅλμον ἐμβληθεὶς καὶ παρανομώτατα συντριβόμενος εὖ μάλα κατεφρόνει τῆς κολάσεως λέγων· „πτίσσε, πτίσσε τὸν Ἀναξάρχου θύλακον, αὐτὸν γὰρ οὐ πτίσσεις“· θείου τινὸς ὡς ἀληθῶς πνεύματος ἡ φωνή. ἀλλὰ καὶ τούτῳ φθάσαντές τινες ἠκολούθησαν φυσικοί, οὐκοῦν Ἐπίκτητον; ὃς τοῦ δεσπότου στρεβλοῦντος αὐτοῦ τὸ σκέλος ὑπομειδιῶν ἀνεκπλήκτως ἔλεγε· „κατάσσεις,“ καὶ κατάξαντος „οὐκ ἔλεγον,“ εἶπεν, „ὅτι κατάσσεις;“ τί τοιοῦτον ὁ ὑμέτερος θεὸς κολαζόμενος ἐφθέγξατο; ὑμεῖς δὲ κἂν Σίβυλλαν. ᾗ χρῶνταί τινες ὑμῶν, εἰκότως αν μᾶλλον προεστήσασθε ὡς τοῦ θεοῦ παῖδα· νῦν δὲ παρεγγράφειν μὲν εἰς τὰ ἐκείνης πολλὰ καὶ βλάσφημα εἰκῇ δύνασθε, τὸν δὲ βίῳ μὲν ἐπιῤῥητοτάτῳ θανάτῳ δὲ οἰκτίστῳ χρησάμενον θεὸν τίθεσθε. πόσῳ τοῦδε ἐπιτηδειότερος ἦν ὑμῖν Ἰωνᾶς „ἐπὶ τῇ κολοκύντῃ“ ἢ Δανιὴλ ὁ ἐκ τῶν θηρίων ἢ οἱ τῶνδε ἔτι τερατωδέστεροι;
pass_a_gloss: After these things, then, to which we have answered (ἀπαντάω) according to ability (κατὰ δύναμιν), he says to us: 'How much better would it have been for you, since you desired (ἐπιθυμέω) to innovate (καινοτομέω) something, to be zealous (σπουδάζω) about another one of those who died (ἀποθνῄσκω) nobly (γενναίως) and are able to receive (δέχομαι) a divine myth (μῦθος)? Come (φέρε), if Heracles and Asclepius and those glorified (δοξάζω) of old did not please (ἀρέσκω), you had Orpheus, a man admittedly (ὁμολογουμένως) having used (χράομαι) a holy (ὅσιος) spirit, and himself having died violently (βιαίως). But perhaps he had been taken beforehand (προλαμβάνω) by others. Anaxarchus, then (γοῦν): who, having been thrown into a mortar (ὅλμος) and being crushed (συντρίβω) most lawlessly (παρανομώτατα), very well despised (καταφρονέω) the punishment (κόλασις), saying: "pound (πτίσσω), pound the bag (θύλακος) of Anaxarchus, for him you do not pound"; the voice of some truly divine spirit. But this one too some natural philosophers (φυσικοί), anticipating (φθάνω), followed (ἀκολουθέω). Epictetus, then (οὐκοῦν)? who, his master (δεσπότης) twisting (στρεβλόω) his leg (σκέλος), smiling (ὑπομειδιάω) unperturbedly (ἀνεκπλήκτως) said: "you are breaking (κατάγνυμι)", and when he had broken it, "did I not say," he said, "that you are breaking?" What such thing did your god utter (φθέγγομαι) being punished (κολάζω)? And you even the Sibyl, whom some of you use, would more fittingly (εἰκότως) have put forward (προΐστημι) as child (παῖς) of God; but now you are able to insert (παρεγγράφω) into hers many and blasphemous (βλάσφημος) things at random (εἰκῇ), and you set up as god the one having had a most infamous (ἐπίρρητος) life and a most pitiable (οἰκτρός) death. How much more fit (ἐπιτήδειος) than this one for you was Jonah "upon the gourd (κολόκυντα)", or Daniel the one from the beasts (θηρία), or those still more portentous (τερατώδης) than these?'
pass_b_english: Next, after these remarks, which we have answered as well as we could, he says to us: “How much better would it have been for you, since you wanted to make some innovation, to have devoted yourselves to someone else among those who died nobly and who could lend themselves to a divine legend? Come, if Heracles and Asclepius and those glorified of old did not please you, you had Orpheus, a man who by common consent had a holy spirit, and who himself also died a violent death. But perhaps others had already claimed him. Anaxarchus, then: thrown into a mortar and pounded in the most lawless way, he utterly scorned the punishment and said, ‘Pound, pound the bag of Anaxarchus; for you are not pounding the man himself.’ Truly the voice of some divine spirit!

“But here too some natural philosophers got there first and followed him. Epictetus, then? When his master was twisting his leg, he smiled and, quite unshaken, said, ‘You will break it’; and when the master had broken it, he said, ‘Did I not tell you that you would break it?’ What did your God say that was like this, while he was being punished? You would even have had more reason to put forward the Sibyl, whom some of you use, as a child of God. As it is, you can recklessly slip many blasphemous things into her writings, yet you set up as God a man whose life was most infamous and whose death was most pitiable. How much more suitable for you than he would Jonah have been, Jonah ‘with the gourd’ (Jonah 4:6), or Daniel, who came out from the beasts (Daniel 6:23), or others still more fantastic than these?”

choices.choice: The whole chapter after the first clause is Celsus’s own wording, set in double quotation marks; the sayings of Anaxarchus and Epictetus within it are in single marks. θεῖον μῦθον δέξασθαι δυναμένων rendered ‘who could carry a divine legend’, that is, about whom a tale of divinity could plausibly be told. ἀλλ᾿ ἴσως ὑπ᾿ ἄλλων προείληπτο: ‘others’ presumably the Orphic sects. φυσικοί taken as natural philosophers (Anaxarchus was a follower of Democritus). κατάσσεις (the usual form would be κατεάξεις) is taken as ‘you will break it’. Celsus says ὁ ὑμέτερος θεός of Jesus; rendered ‘your God’ with a capital, since he means the One whom Christians worship. κολόκυνθα is the Septuagint ‘gourd’ of Jonah 4:6 (English Bibles often ‘plant’). ‘Daniel, who came out from the beasts’ alludes to the lions’ den, Daniel 6:23; the second lions’ den story (Bel and the Dragon 31–42) is also possible. τερατωδέστεροι rendered ‘more fantastic’ to keep Celsus’s sneer, which Origen takes up in 7.57. The anecdotes of Anaxarchus and Epictetus are told by Celsus without naming a source; no classical citation is given. Review: ἐπὶ τῇ κολοκύντῃ is the Septuagint phrase of Jonah 4:6 and 4:9 (‘rejoiced over the gourd’, ‘grieved over the gourd’); ‘under the gourd’ was wrong, so it is rendered neutrally ‘with the gourd’. κἄν before Σίβυλλαν (‘even the Sibyl’) restored. εἰκῇ rendered ‘recklessly’ rather than ‘at random’. Celsus’s opening sentence is a question in the Greek and is kept as one. Daniel 6:23 is the English numbering; the Greek (Theodotion) and Aramaic number it 6:24.
opening: 'After this, then, to which' -> 'Next, after these remarks, which'
Celsus's first sentence kept as a question, not an exclamation; σπουδάσαι περί 'taken up the cause of' -> 'devoted yourselves to'; δέξασθαι 'carry' -> 'lend themselves to'
Anaxarchus saying: 'for him you are not pounding' -> 'for you are not pounding the man himself'
'What did your God utter like this' -> 'What did your God say that was like this'
κἄν ('even') restored before the Sibyl; εἰκῇ 'at random' -> 'recklessly'; μέν ... δέ contrast marked with 'yet'
ἐπὶ τῇ κολοκύντῃ: 'under the gourd' (wrong preposition sense) -> 'with the gourd'

choices.choice: 7.53: pass_a_gloss fields were not rewritten. They still give the literal sense (for example 'upon the gourd' in 7.53), while the English and notes now carry the corrected readings.

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
